comment: Human-review record for the mass extraction of WD-lws10-core-20260622. Every extracted block index (i) is either seeded (hand-written in the catalog before Gate 1), skipped (with reason), or curated below (slug + summary; level auto-derived from the strongest BCP 14 keyword unless overridden). tools/extractor/emit_candidates.py turns this into catalog entries.

skip.1: BCP 14 boilerplate - defines keyword interpretation, not a conformance clause

entries.summary: An LWS Server is an HTTP server that complies with all relevant MUST statements, specifically those in the Operations section.
An LWS Client is an HTTP client that complies with all relevant MUST statements, specifically those in the Operations section.
An authentication credential includes tamper-evident claims about a subject.
The subject claim is required and its value is a URI.
The issuer claim is required and its value is a URI.
The client claim is required and should be a URI.
Audience restriction is recommended and its list should include an authorization server identifier.
Verifier-issuer trust may be established out of band; authentication suites define additional mechanisms.
Authentication credentials are signed; asymmetric cryptography is recommended.
Each authentication suite is associated with a token type URI, preferably from the IANA OAuth URI registry.
OAuth 2.0 is the baseline authorization framework; servers may support additional mechanisms.
A storage server generating a 401 sends a WWW-Authenticate header with at least one conforming challenge.
The as_uri challenge parameter is required and identifies the authorization server that issues access tokens.
The realm challenge parameter is required; clients verify the request URI is logically within the realm.
Challenges may include other headers and parameters.
Authorization servers provide RFC 8414 metadata at /.well-known/lws-configuration.
Server metadata should advertise supported subject token types via subject_token_types_supported.
The token endpoint supports the RFC 8693 token-exchange grant type.
The resource parameter is a required URI that populates aud; requests naming unknown or untrusted storages are rejected.
The subject_token parameter is required and carries a valid subject token such as an authentication credential.
All presented tokens are validated before an access token is returned.
Token responses conform to RFC 6749 section 5.1; access tokens conform to RFC 9068.
The access token sub claim is a required URI identifying the acting agent.
The access token iss claim is required and is the authorization server URI.
The access token client_id claim is a required URI identifying the client.
The access token aud claim includes the resource-parameter URI (the storage realm).
The exp claim is required; short lifetimes are recommended (300 seconds or less).
The iat claim is required.
The jti claim is required.
Invalid or unauthorized token requests produce RFC 6749 section 5.2 error responses.
Clients present access tokens via the Authorization header per RFC 6750.
Storage servers validate access tokens with the defined checks, rejecting the request on any failure.
JWT signatures are verified against the jwks_uri from server metadata; keys should be cached and key rotation is supported.
Failed validation yields 401 with a WWW-Authenticate error parameter such as invalid_token.
A valid token whose authorization policy disallows the operation is rejected.
The storage description id is a required URI identifying the storage.
The storage description type equals or includes the string Storage (case-sensitive).
A capability object id, if present, is a URI.
A capability object type is a required string or set of strings.
The capability property, if present, is a set of capability maps; additional properties are allowed.
A service object id, if present, is a URI.
A service object type is a required string or set of strings.
A service object serviceEndpoint is a required URI.
The service property is a required set of service maps; additional properties are allowed.
GET/HEAD responses on storage resources include a Link header rel=lws#storageDescription pointing at the storage description.
A dereferenced storage description has an id identifying the storage and a StorageDescription service entry whose serviceEndpoint is its own URL.
Storage descriptions serialize as application/lws+json; other representations may be negotiable.
Containers support ContainerPage pagination (first/next/prev/last) and represent as JSON-LD with the normative frame and context.
Containment is expressed via a Link header rel=up on GET and HEAD responses of any non-root resource.
The server maintains containment integrity at all times.
Creating a resource atomically adds it to the parent container items list.
Deleting a resource atomically removes it from the parent items list; container deletion requires emptiness unless recursion is requested.
Every non-root resource is reachable from the storage root through the containment hierarchy.
A container never directly or indirectly contains itself.
URIs are server-assigned (Slug may hint); clients should not assume URI structure reflects containment.
A readable container lists all members the client can access and may include members the client cannot access.
A container representation includes the required property set defined by the Containers section.
totalItems is the disclosable contained-resource count; it should be accurate but may be approximate.
Each items entry includes the required contained-resource description members.
Contained-resource descriptions should include the recommended members.
The mediaType member is present for DataResources in container listings.
Servers support the four core operations, handling each atomically and consistently; error responses inform without leaking sensitive detail.
Per-resource metadata links are available as a standalone linkset resource per RFC 9264.
Linkset resources are available as application/linkset+json.
The linkset link targets a server-managed resource; linkset updates are atomic with the associated resource operations.
Relevant responses carry a Link header rel=storageDescription.
Clients may use Prefer with lws#PreferLinkRelations to include or omit specific relations.
Core metadata may be client-modifiable; servers advertise their capabilities via standard HTTP headers.
Servers advertise GET and PATCH support on the linkset resource via the Allow header.
Optional PUT or alternative patch formats, when supported, appear in Allow and Accept-Patch.
Clients do not assume PUT or patch-format support unless advertised, and handle 405 and 415 gracefully.
Metadata is managed via the linkset resource URI; servers support concurrency controls for updates.
PATCH with application/merge-patch+json is the primary metadata-management mechanism on the linkset.
PUT may replace the entire linkset if advertised; otherwise the server rejects it with 405 Method Not Allowed.
Servers may restrict modification of specific links (such as up or items) to maintain integrity.
Deleting a resource automatically removes its associated linkset metadata.
POST creates with a server-assigned identifier (Slug and client Link metadata allowed); server-managed metadata is generated automatically and never overridden by client links.
The server may honor the Slug header when it does not conflict with naming rules or existing resources.
POST is not idempotent; clients should avoid unintentional retries or use unique identifiers.
The linkset resource is created and populated with mandatory server-managed fields before creation success is returned.
401 responses should include a Link header rel=storageDescription for discoverability.
A container GET returns a member listing that may be authorization-filtered, with core metadata per member.
Servers distinguish resource types via metadata; all read responses integrate Link headers rel=linkset, rel=up and rel=type, atomically with resource state.
Container listings include member identifiers and types (required), media types for DataResources (required), and sizes and timestamps (recommended).
Container read responses include an ETag representing the listing version plus Link headers rel=type, rel=linkset and rel=up.
401 responses should carry WWW-Authenticate parameters that guide clients without hardcoded URIs.
PUT/PATCH on a resource URI modify content only; combined content+metadata updates are opt-in via Prefer: set-linkset (optional for servers; otherwise ignored or 501).
Successful updates respond 200 or 204 and should include the new ETag.
Linkset writes use optimistic concurrency: ETag on reads, new ETag after writes, If-Match required (mismatch yields 412, absence yields 428).
DELETE targets the resource URI; clients may include If-Match for concurrency checks.
Successful DELETE responds 204 No Content; conditional requests should be supported.
Unauthorized deletes yield 403 for a known identity with insufficient permission or 401 without valid authentication; 404 may hide existence.
201 responses carry Location, an ETag for concurrency, and server-managed Link headers.
204 indicates success without a body; servers may use 410 Gone for permanent deletions.
Error responses should use the RFC 9457 problem-details format.
Advertised access endpoints use service objects typed AccessRequestService / AccessGrantService, with conformsTo listing supported access profiles.
Other properties may be present on access requests and access grants.
The type value includes AccessRequest for requests or AccessGrant for grants; additional types are allowed.
The type property on access requests and grants is required.
The storage property value is a URI.
The storage property is required.
The inbox property value is a URI.
The inbox property is optional.
The access property is a collection of one or more objects.
The access property is required.
A policy type includes AccessPolicy; additional types are allowed.
The policy type property is required.
The action property is a collection of server-recognized operation strings; read, modify, create and delete are mandatory to support.
The action property is required.
The assignee is a URI; public access may be assigned via foaf:Agent.
The assignee property is required.
The target property is an object containing the defined properties.
Servers may support additional target type values.
The target property is optional.
The constraint property, if present, is a collection of constraint objects with the defined members.
When multiple constraint objects are present, all must be satisfied.
Servers advertising this profile support the defined leftOperand values.
The constraint property is optional.
All constraint objects must be satisfied for access to be permitted.
Access request/grant JSON-LD documents include an @context ordered set containing https://www.w3.org/ns/lws/v1; extension contexts are allowed.
Access request and grant endpoints are LWS containers conforming to this specification.
Access endpoints minimally support GET and POST; DELETE is recommended; other operations may be supported.
Access endpoints support the JSON-LD serialization for request and response payloads; other serializations may be added.
A successful POST to an access endpoint responds with a Location header for the new resource.
When an inbox property is present, the server should deliver notifications to that endpoint.
Notification serialization conforms to the LWS notification data model.
Inbox notifications conform to the LWS notification delivery requirements.
Servers should send notifications for the defined access lifecycle events.
The storage controller should be notified when a new access request is submitted.
The requesting agent should be notified at the access-request inbox when a grant is created.
Servers may send notifications for other events.
Container representations and storage description resources use the media type application/lws+json.
application/ld+json with the lws/v1 profile should be treated as equivalent to application/lws+json.
Container content negotiation returns an identical payload across media types; only the Content-Type header varies.
A request for application/lws+json is answered with Content-Type: application/lws+json.
A request for application/ld+json is answered with Content-Type: application/ld+json.
A request for application/json is answered with Content-Type: application/json.
Servers should paginate containers whose membership exceeds a server-determined threshold.
rel=first is present on paginated responses.
rel=last may be present on paginated responses.
rel=next is present when subsequent pages exist and omitted on the last page.
rel=prev may be present with preceding pages and is omitted on the first page.
Pagination URIs are opaque; clients use the URIs the server provides.
The composite resource URI yields the first page; servers may support direct access to specific pages.
Paginated responses are 200 OK; totalItems should reflect the total across all pages.
Container representations include the normative @context value.
Per the IANA registration, application/ld+json with the lws/v1 profile should be treated as equivalent to application/lws+json.
